title: Why 'learning styles' is a myth
keyIdea: Many people believe each person is a visual, auditory or kinaesthetic learner and learns more when lessons match that style. Careful tests have not found this: matching lessons to a style label does not raise scores. What does help is choosing the method that fits the topic, mixing words with pictures, and testing yourself. Having a favourite way to learn is real, but it does not decide how well you learn.

kid: You may have heard that some people are visual learners, some are listening learners and some learn by doing. The idea says you learn more when a lesson is given in your own style. Lots of people believe it, and some schools have even tested children to find their style.

Scientists checked this idea properly. They gave picture lovers and listening lovers the same lesson, shown either as a picture or in spoken words. If styles were real, each group would win with its own method. That did not happen. When the topic was a map, nearly everyone did better with the picture.

So what really decides the best way? The topic does. A map is best seen. The sound of a French word is best heard. Tying a knot is best done with your hands. That is true for every learner, whatever they like best.

Some tricks help almost everyone. Putting words and pictures together gives your memory two clues instead of one. Testing yourself, then checking your answers, beats reading your notes again. And having a favourite way to learn is fine. Just do not let a label stop you trying the way that fits.
adult: Many people believe children learn best when teaching matches their visual, auditory or kinaesthetic (VAK) style. Surveys of teachers in the UK and other countries found over 80% agree. In 2008, Pashler and colleagues asked what a fair test would look like. Matched groups would need to beat mismatched groups. They found almost no studies that did this well, and most of those went against the idea.

A common mistake is to treat a liking as an ability. Children do have likes, and they are worth hearing. But a child's stated style does not predict which method helps them most. Calling a child 'a kinaesthetic learner' can narrow what they try. They may skip reading because 'it is not my style'.

This fits under metacognition and self-regulated learning, the EEF's term for planning, checking and reviewing your own learning. Better methods have good evidence. Dual coding pairs words with diagrams. Retrieval practice means testing yourself. Spacing spreads study out. Pick the mode the topic needs: diagrams for shapes and maps, audio for how words sound, and hands-on practice for physical skills.

The lab uses made-up scores that follow the direction of the research. Your child meets three learners with real likes and runs a fair test on learning a map. Then they match topics to methods and compare words alone with words plus pictures. Last, they try three study plans to see which one lasts a week.

familyTip: Next time your child says 'I'm just not a reading person' or similar, try one small swap: learn five facts from a page that has a diagram, cover it up, and see how many you can both say back. Talk about how the picture and the testing helped, not the style.

items: Test yourself, then check your answers
Only learn from pictures because you are a visual learner
Add a labelled diagram to your notes
Skip reading because it is not your style
Listen to how a new word sounds
Take a quiz to find your one learning style
Use your hands to practise a new skill like knitting
Lessons only work when they match your style

lab.caption: Flagship lab: meet three learners, test the learning-styles claim, match topics to methods, and find what helps everyone remember.

practice.prompt: Sam says he is a listening learner. He needs to learn the shape of Italy for a test. What is the best way?
choices: Look at a map of Italy
Listen to someone describe it
Act out the shape with his arms
practice.hint: Ask what the topic needs, not what Sam likes.
practice.explain: A shape is best learned from a picture. Sam can learn from a map just as well as anyone, whatever his favourite way is.

practice.prompt: In a test, picture lovers scored {a} out of 10 with a picture and {b} out of 10 with words. How many more did they score with the picture?
practice.hint: Take the words score away from the picture score.
practice.explain: {a} - {b} = {=a-b}. The same gap showed for the listening lovers too, so the topic, not the style, made the difference.

practice.prompt: You remember {a} facts from words only, and {b} more when pictures are added. How many facts do you remember with words and pictures?
practice.hint: Add the extra facts to the words-only score.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. Pairing words with pictures gives your memory two clues, and that helps almost everyone.

practice.prompt: Which study plan is backed by research for every learner?
choices: Testing yourself, then checking
Studying only in your learning style
Re-reading until it feels familiar
practice.hint: Which plan makes your brain pull the answer back out?
practice.explain: Testing yourself makes you pull facts out of memory, which makes them last. Matching a style and re-reading did not do better.

pool.prompt: What does the learning-styles idea claim?
choices: You learn more when lessons match your style
Everyone learns in exactly the same way
Pictures never help
pool.hint: It is about matching lessons to a label.
pool.explain: The claim is that matching a lesson to your visual, listening or doing style makes you learn more. Careful tests did not find this.

pool.prompt: Picture lovers and listening lovers both scored higher with a picture of a map. What does that show?
choices: The topic decided the best method
Only picture lovers can read maps
Listening lovers did the test wrong
pool.hint: Both groups won with the same method.
pool.explain: If styles mattered, each group would win with its own method. Both won with the picture, so the topic decided.

pool.prompt: Which topic is best learned by listening?
choices: How a bird song sounds
The layout of a football pitch
How to ride a bike
pool.hint: Ask what the thing to be learned is: a sound, a shape or a movement.
pool.explain: A sound has to be heard, so listening fits best for everyone. A layout is best seen, and riding is best done.

pool.prompt: A quiz tells Tom he is a visual learner. What should his teacher do?
choices: Use the method that fits each topic, as for everyone
Teach Tom only with pictures
Move Tom to a picture-only group
pool.hint: Did matching lessons to a style label help in careful tests?
pool.explain: Matching lessons to a style label did not raise scores in careful tests. Tom learns best, like everyone, when the method fits the topic.

pool.prompt: Lena says, 'I'm a doing learner, so I won't bother reading.' What is the best advice?
choices: Reading still works for you, so keep trying it
Yes, only learn by doing
Read only when the teacher watches
pool.hint: Does a preference switch off other ways to learn?
pool.explain: A style label can stop people trying methods that work. Lena can learn from reading like anyone else.

pool.prompt: Which helps almost everyone remember more?
choices: Words and pictures together
Learning only in your favourite way
Highlighting the whole page
pool.hint: Think about giving your memory two different kinds of clue for one idea.
pool.explain: Pairing words with pictures gives memory two routes back to the idea. It helps most learners, not just picture lovers.

pool.prompt: A week later, re-reading left {a} facts remembered and testing yourself left {b}. How many more facts did testing yourself leave?
pool.hint: Take the re-reading score from the testing score.
pool.explain: {b} - {a} = {=b-a}. Pulling answers out of memory makes them last longer than reading again.

pool.prompt: Is it fine to have a favourite way to learn?
choices: Yes, but the topic should still choose the method
No, favourites are made up
Yes, so use it for every topic
pool.hint: Likes are real. Do they make you learn more?
pool.explain: Your likes are real and worth knowing. They just do not make you learn more, so pick the method that fits the topic.

pool.prompt: In the lab test, 'listening' kids scored {a} out of 10 with a map picture and {b} out of 10 when the map was described in words. How many more marks did the picture give them?
pool.hint: Take the words score away from the picture score.
pool.explain: {a} - {b} = {=a-b}. Even the 'listening' kids did better with the picture, because a map is a picture-y topic.
